objective: By the end of this lesson you can tell, for any flight, whether you are legal to act as pilot in command: right certificate and endorsements, current flight review and landings, a valid medical or BasicMed, and the right documents on board.
why: Being legal is the floor, not the goal. You must know the rules cold, and also know when you are legal but not ready to fly safely.

prereading.what: What a private pilot may and may not do, plus the BasicMed conditions in 61.113(i).
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.113

prereading.what: Flight review and passenger-carrying landing currency.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.56 and 61.57

prereading.what: Medical certificate duration table. Find the private pilot rows.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.23(d)

prereading.what: Why currency is a minimum, and what a flight review is for.
prereading.label: AC 61-98E, 3-1 to 4-2

prereading.what: How to plan your transition to an unfamiliar airplane and reduce its risks.
prereading.label: AC 90-109A, 5g to 6a

warmup: You passed your checkride 2 years ago and have flown 3 times since. Your friend asks for a ride tonight in a club airplane you have never flown. What would you need to check before you say yes?

key_terms.def: The pilot who is in charge of and responsible for the flight.
Meeting the minimum recent-experience rules (flight review, 3 takeoffs and landings, etc.) so you are legal.
Actually having the skill and knowledge to fly this flight safely, today.
At least 1 hour ground and 1 hour flight training with an instructor, required every 24 calendar months to act as PIC.
Counts to the end of the month. A deadline in a calendar month runs to the last day of that month.
A signed logbook entry from an authorized instructor saying you got specific training (e.g., complex, high-performance, tailwheel).
A way to act as PIC (or required flightcrew member) without an FAA medical certificate, using a U.S. driver's license, a doctor exam, and an online course (14 CFR 61.113(i) and Part 68).
An equal share. A private pilot may not pay less than an equal share of fuel, oil, airport fees, or rental.

chunks.title: How you earn the private pilot certificate

body.p: To be eligible for a private pilot certificate (airplane) you must meet these rules in [[60:294|14 CFR 61.103]]:

bullets: Be at least 17 years old [[60:294|14 CFR 61.103(a)]].
Read, speak, write, and understand English [[60:295|14 CFR 61.103(c)]].
Get an instructor endorsement, then pass the knowledge test [[60:295|14 CFR 61.103(d)-(e)]].
Get flight training and an instructor endorsement for the practical test [[60:295|14 CFR 61.103(f)]].
Meet the aeronautical experience rules, then pass the practical test [[60:295|14 CFR 61.103(g)-(h)]].
Hold a student, sport, or recreational pilot certificate [[60:295|14 CFR 61.103(j)]].

body.p: For airplane single-engine, you need at least 40 hours of flight time, with at least 20 hours of training from an instructor and 10 hours of solo [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)]].

head: Required training (minimum)
Amount
rows: 3 hours, incl. one cross-country over 100 NM total and 10 full-stop takeoffs and landings
3 hours, within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test
150 NM total, full-stop landings at 3 points, one leg over 50 NM straight-line

callout.text: Your pilot certificate has no expiration date. It stays valid unless surrendered, suspended, or revoked [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(a), (c)]]. What expires is your currency and your medical.

check.q: Does a private pilot certificate expire?
check.a: No. It is issued without an expiration date and is valid unless surrendered, suspended, or revoked [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19]].

body.p: To act as PIC, you must have done a flight review since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month you fly. The review is given by an authorized instructor, in an aircraft you are rated for, and you need a logbook endorsement for it [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].
A flight review is at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training. It covers the Part 91 rules and the maneuvers the instructor picks [[60:236|14 CFR 61.56(a)]].

bullets: A checkride for a new pilot certificate or rating counts as a flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)]].
Finishing one or more phases of the FAA WINGS program also counts [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(e)]], [[15:23|AC 61-98E 4-2]].
A student pilot with a current solo endorsement does not need one [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(g)]].

callout.text: Count calendar months. Review done March 15, 2025? You may act as PIC through March 31, 2027. On April 1, 2027 you need a new one.

body.p: A flight review is not a pass/fail test. It is training where your skill is checked. If you are not ready, the instructor gives more training before signing it off [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4-1]]. If you do not get the endorsement, you may keep flying only until your old 24-month period runs out [[15:29|AC 61-98E 4-8]].

check.q: Your last flight review was signed June 10, 2025. What is the last day you can act as PIC without a new one?
check.a: June 30, 2027, the end of the 24th calendar month [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].

body.p: To be PIC of an aircraft carrying persons, you need 3 takeoffs and 3 landings within the preceding 90 days. You must be the sole manipulator of the controls, in the same category, class, and type (if a class or type rating is required) [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]].

head: Rule
Day
Night
rows: Carrying persons from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise

body.p: Source: [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a) and (b)]]. In a tailwheel airplane, the 3 landings must be to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

callout.text: Not current? You can still fly solo to get current, day VFR or day IFR, with no persons or property on board other than what the flight needs [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(2)]].

body.p: The rule counts by category and class (and type only if a type rating is required) [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]]. Landings in a Cessna 152 keep you legal in a Cessna 172. The FAA still recommends getting current in each make and model before carrying passengers [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3-1]].

check.q: You made 3 touch-and-go landings at dusk 30 days ago. Can you take a friend flying at 2100, two hours after sunset?
check.a: No. Night passenger currency needs 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop, done between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise, within 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

body.p: You must log the training and experience you use to meet the rules for a certificate, rating, or flight review, and the experience you use for recent flight experience [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]].
Each logged flight needs at least [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]]:

bullets: Date
Total flight or lesson time
Departure and arrival location
Type and identification of aircraft (or simulator/training device)
Name of safety pilot, if one was required

body.p: You must show your pilot certificate, medical certificate, logbook, or other required record when reasonably asked by the FAA, an NTSB representative, or any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

callout.text: Moved? You may not use your certificate more than 30 days after a change of permanent mailing address unless you notify the FAA Airman Certification Branch in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

check.q: Why does the flight review endorsement matter so much in your logbook?
check.a: The rule requires a logbook endorsement from the instructor who gave the review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)(2)]], and you must present your logbook on reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)]]. No entry, no proof.

body.p: The basic rule: a private pilot may not act as PIC of an aircraft carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire, and may not act as PIC for compensation or hire [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]].
The exceptions in [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(b)-(h)]], plus BasicMed in [[60:308|61.113(i)]]:

head: You may...
As long as...
rows: Fly for your business or job
The flight is only incidental to it, and no passengers or property are carried for hire (b)
You pay at least your pro rata share, and costs are only fuel, oil, airport fees, or rental fees (c)
Fly a charitable, nonprofit, or community event flight
Be reimbursed for search and location flights
Only fuel, oil, airport fees, or rental, and sanctioned by an agency or search organization (e)
Demonstrate an airplane as a salesman
You have at least 200 hours logged flight time (f)
Tow a glider or unpowered ultralight

body.p: The PHAK sums it up: a private pilot flies for pleasure or personal business and may not be paid for pilot services, though passengers can pay a pro rata share of expenses [[1:33|PHAK 1-18]].

To be PIC you must hold the right category, class, and type rating (if required) for the aircraft [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(d)]]. Your ASEL certificate does not let you be PIC of a multiengine airplane or seaplane. The only exception is solo flight while training for that rating, with an instructor's solo endorsement, and never with passengers [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(c), (d)(2)]].

callout.text: No instrument rating means no PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]].

check.q: You fly 3 friends to the beach. Fuel and rental cost $400. What is the least you can pay?
check.a: $100. You are one of 4 people, so your pro rata share is one fourth [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]].

body.p: Some airplanes need extra training and a one-time logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor before you can act as PIC [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)-(f)]].

head: Airplane
What it means
Requirement
rows: Retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller (or FADEC) [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]]
Ground and flight training plus a one-time endorsement [[60:213|61.31(e)]]
An engine of more than 200 horsepower
Ground and flight training plus a one-time endorsement [[60:213|61.31(f)]]
Service ceiling or max operating altitude (lower one) above 25,000 feet MSL
Ground training plus endorsement, and flight training in a pressurized aircraft plus endorsement [[60:214|61.31(g)(1)-(2)]]
Flight training (normal and crosswind takeoffs/landings, wheel landings, go-arounds) plus endorsement [[60:215|61.31(i)]]

callout.text: Complex = Gear up, Flaps, and Prop control. High-performance = more than 200 HP. Each needs its own endorsement.

check.q: Your friend's airplane has a 230 HP engine, fixed gear, and a constant-speed prop. What endorsement do you need?
check.a: High-performance, because the engine is more than 200 HP [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. It is not complex because the gear does not retract [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]].

body.p: A private pilot needs at least a third-class medical, unless flying under BasicMed [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)]]. Medicals come from an aviation medical examiner (AME). There are three classes [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].

A medical expires at the end of the last day of the month shown below, counted from the month of the exam. Which date applies depends on what privileges you use and your age on the exam date [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]].

head: Class
Used for
Under 40
40 or older
rows: Private, recreational, student, CFI as PIC

callout.text: A higher class medical drops down. A first-class medical that is too old for airline use can still be good for private privileges [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].
Example: third-class exam on June 10, 2026 at age 35 is good for private flying through June 30, 2031. At age 45 it would be good through June 30, 2028.

check.q: You are 42. Your third-class exam was in March 2026. Through what date can you use it as a private pilot?
check.a: March 31, 2028, the end of the 24th month after the exam month [[60:210|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(ii)]].

body.p: Holding a medical certificate is not enough. You may not act as PIC while you know or have reason to know of a medical condition that would make you unable to meet your medical standards, or while taking medication or treatment that makes you unable to meet them [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. Under BasicMed (driver's license), the rule is: no acting as PIC while you know or have reason to know of any medical condition that would make you unable to fly the aircraft safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b), (c)(2)]].
Alcohol and drugs rules [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. No acting as a crewmember:

bullets: Within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol
While under the influence of alcohol
While using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety
With an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater

body.p: Alcohol lasts longer than you think. The body needs about 3 hours to clear one beer or one mixed drink. A hangover still means you are under the influence, and alcohol can stay in the body over 16 hours [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Medication: many over-the-counter cold and allergy drugs, like diphenhydramine, cause drowsiness that lasts a long time. The condition being treated may itself be disqualifying [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

callout.text: IMSAFE before every flight: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

check.q: You had one beer 9 hours ago and feel fine. Legal?
check.a: Legal by the 8-hour rule only if your alcohol concentration is below 0.04 and you are not under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. The PHAK says it is wise to be more conservative than the rules [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

body.p: To act as a required pilot, these must be in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft:

bullets: Your pilot certificate (or temporary certificate) [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]
Photo ID: driver's license, government ID card, U.S. Armed Forces ID, passport, or other accepted ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]], [[60:189|61.3(a)(2)(v)-(vi)]]
Your medical certificate, unless you fly under an exception such as BasicMed [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]
Under BasicMed: a U.S. driver's license [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)]], with the BasicMed course certificate and exam checklist in your logbook [[60:308|61.113(i)(3)]]

body.p: You must show these, with your photo ID, on request of the FAA, an NTSB representative, any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer, or a TSA representative [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]], [[60:194|61.3(l)(3)-(4)]].

callout.text: Pilot carries 3 things: Pilot certificate, Photo ID, and Medical (or driver's license for BasicMed).

check.q: You left your pilot certificate at home but have your medical and driver's license. Can you act as PIC?
check.a: No. Your pilot certificate must be in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]].

body.p: BasicMed lets a private pilot act as PIC without an FAA medical certificate [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]. To use it you must [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]]:

bullets: Hold a valid U.S. driver's license and follow its restrictions

Have held an FAA medical certificate at any point after July 14, 2006. It may be expired (or a special issuance), but not suspended or revoked. Your most recent special issuance authorization cannot have been withdrawn, and your most recent medical application cannot have been completed and denied [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(ii)-(iv)]]
Complete the BasicMed medical education course within the past 24 calendar months
Get a comprehensive medical exam from a State-licensed physician within the past 48 calendar months, using the FAA checklist (CMEC)
Be under a physician's care for any diagnosed condition that may affect your ability to fly

head: BasicMed limit (current rule)
Value
rows: Inside the U.S. unless authorized by the country where the flight is

body.p: Source: [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)-(2)]]. Your logbook must contain the completed exam checklist and the course completion certificate [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

callout.text: AC 68-1A (2017) lists older limits: 6 occupants, 6,000 pounds, 5 passengers, and no flying for compensation [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3-1]]. The current regulation (14 CFR as of 10/08/2026) raised these to 7 occupants, 12,500 pounds, 6 passengers. Always use the current regulation. Private pilot limits on compensation in 61.113(a) still apply.

body.p: Under the current rule, BasicMed lets a private pilot act as PIC or serve as a required flightcrew member [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]. (AC 68-1A, written earlier, says PIC only [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4-1]].) It does not cover commercial or ATP privileges, which need a first- or second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(1)-(2)]], [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4-1]]. A passport works as photo ID but cannot replace the driver's license for BasicMed [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4-1]].

check.q: Your BasicMed course was done 26 calendar months ago and your doctor exam 30 months ago. Can you fly under BasicMed?
check.a: No. The course must be within 24 calendar months [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)]]. The exam is fine (48 calendar months).

body.p: Currency asks: did you log the minimum events the rules require? Proficiency asks: can you actually handle the conditions of this flight? Being current does not guarantee you can handle the flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

The FAA calls the 61.57 landing rules minimums. A pilot current only in light winds on long runways should get more practice before carrying passengers in strong wind or on a short runway [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3-1]].
Build a personal currency program that goes beyond the minimums, such as extra landings or short-field and soft-field practice on normal flights [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1-4]].

Use personal minimums. When you lack currency (for example, you have not flown for several weeks) or face other added risk, raise your baseline minimums [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Set them when you are calm, not while under pressure to fly [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: You are legal to fly but have not flown in 7 weeks and winds are gusty. What does a good pilot do?
check.a: Recognize that currency is not proficiency. Raise personal minimums, fly solo or with an instructor first, or wait for better weather [[30:17|RMH 2-5]], [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3-1]].

body.p: Accident rates go up for pilots with little or no time in the aircraft type they fly. The FAA recommends a full checkout from an instructor in each make and model, and knowing its POH/AFM [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3-1]].

The FAA's guide for this is AC 90-109A, Transition to Unfamiliar Aircraft. It says pilots moving to an unfamiliar airplane need specific training in its systems and its normal, abnormal and emergency procedures [[57:1|AC 90-109A 3a]]. The risk goes both ways: moving down to a slower, simpler airplane is as risky as moving up [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]].

Best training choice: the airplane you will actually fly, with a well-qualified instructor who, preferably, has recent experience in that make and model. Second best: the same make and model [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]]. Before you fly, know the airplane's systems, limits and procedures, especially its instruments, avionics and autopilot [[57:9|AC 90-109A 6c(1)]].

bullets: Get training in your airplane or a similar one [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a(3)(a)]].
Build up slowly; don't take on conditions, like strong crosswinds, you are not ready for [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a(3)(e)]].
Limit who flies with you until you know the airplane, except for instruction [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a(3)(h)]].
Set personal minimums based on your experience [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a(3)(j)]].

body.p: Glass cockpits and autopilots help, but you must be proficient with them and know their limits [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2-4]]. Learn the systems before you fly. The FAA strongly recommends a thorough evaluation from an instructor who knows that aircraft's automation [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2-5]].

Relying on automation can erode your hand-flying skills. Fly by hand at times, and if the automation does something unexpected, reduce the automation level and fly the airplane [[30:51|RMH 7-2]], [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2-5]].

bullets: Anticipate: know what should happen before you push a button.
Act: push the button or turn the knob.
Verify: make sure the airplane does what you expected.

body.p: Source: [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. A pilot without enough training may not expect a mode change, such as the autopilot dropping to wings-level when the navigation source changes [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

check.q: Your club adds a new airplane with a different GPS and autopilot. You are current in category and class. What should you do before carrying passengers?
check.a: Get a checkout from an instructor who knows that airplane and avionics, preferably with recent make-and-model experience, study the POH/AFM, and practice manual flying and automation use [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3-1]], [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]], [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2-5]].

chunks.title: Checkride skill: Can I be PIC?

body.p: The examiner will give you a scenario and ask if you can legally act as PIC under VFR. Work through it in order:

head: Check
Question
Rule
rows: 3 takeoffs/landings in 90 days? Night full stops?
Valid for private privileges at your age? Or BasicMed met?
Any condition, medication, or alcohol issue?
Pilot certificate, photo ID, medical or driver's license?
Any compensation? Cost sharing pro rata?

callout.text: Answer with the rule and the reason. Then add the safety view: legal, but am I proficient for this flight?

check.q: What are the two parts of a strong answer to an examiner's PIC scenario?
check.a: First, whether you are legal and which rule says so. Second, whether you are proficient and safe for that flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

scenario.title: Saturday night trip to dinner
scenario.setup: It is Saturday, October 17, 2026. You earned your private pilot certificate (ASEL) on May 20, 2025, and that checkride is your most recent flight review event. You are 44. Your third-class medical exam was in February 2025. Your last flights were 3 daytime touch-and-go landings in a Cessna 172 with analog gauges 70 days ago. Two friends want you to fly them to a restaurant 80 NM away, leaving at sunset and returning at 2200. The only airplane available is a club Cessna 182 (230 HP, fixed gear, constant-speed prop) with a glass cockpit and autopilot you have never used. One friend offers to pay for all the fuel.

questions.a: Yes. The checkride on May 20, 2025 counts [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)]] and is good through May 31, 2027 [[60:237|61.56(c)]].
Yes, for now. You were 40 or older at the exam, so for private privileges it expires at the end of the 24th month after February 2025: February 28, 2027 [[60:210|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(ii)]].

questions.q: Can you carry the friends on the return leg at 2200?
questions.a: No. Your touch-and-goes do not meet night currency: you need 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise within 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. Your 3 daytime landings 70 days ago do cover day passenger currency [[60:238|61.57(a)]].
Not as PIC without a high-performance endorsement, since 230 HP is more than 200 HP [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. It is not complex because the gear is fixed [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]].

questions.q: Can your friend pay for all the fuel?
questions.a: No. You must pay at least your pro rata share, here one third [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]].

questions.q: Even after you get the endorsement and night landings, what risks remain?
questions.a: An unfamiliar airplane and glass avionics, at night, with passengers. Accident rates go up with little time in type [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3-1]]. Get an instructor checkout on the avionics [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2-5]], raise your personal minimums [[30:17|RMH 2-5]], or pick a day trip in the 172 instead.

skills.do: Given a scenario by the examiner, decide whether you can legally act as PIC under VFR. Check certificate and ratings, endorsements, flight review, day and night passenger currency, medical or BasicMed, fitness to fly, documents, and cost sharing. Cite the rule for each answer and say whether the flight is also safe.
skills.practice: Run the 8-step PIC checklist on your own logbook today. Then have a friend or your CFI make up 5 scenarios (different ages, dates, airplanes, night/day, passengers) and answer each out loud with the regulation number in under 2 minutes.

quiz.q: A private pilot may act as PIC carrying passengers only if, within the preceding 90 days, the pilot has made:
options: 3 takeoffs and 3 landings as sole manipulator in the same category and class
1 takeoff and 1 landing in any aircraft
3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop at night
5 takeoffs and 5 landings with an instructor
quiz.why: Day passenger currency is 3 takeoffs and 3 landings in the same category, class, and type (if required) within 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: Night passenger currency counts takeoffs and landings made during what period?
options: Sunset to sunrise
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
Civil twilight
30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise
quiz.why: They must be to a full stop between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

quiz.q: A pilot under 40 gets a third-class medical on January 5, 2026. For private privileges it expires at the end of:
options: January 31, 2028
January 5, 2031
January 31, 2031
December 31, 2030
quiz.why: Under 40, a medical used for private privileges expires at the end of the last day of the 60th month after the exam month [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(i)]].

quiz.q: What is the minimum flight review?
options: 1 hour flight training only
1 hour ground and 1 hour flight training
2 hours ground and 2 hours flight
A practical test with an examiner
quiz.why: A flight review is at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training [[60:236|14 CFR 61.56(a)]].

quiz.q: A high-performance airplane is one with:
options: Retractable gear
An engine of more than 200 horsepower
A constant-speed propeller
A service ceiling above 25,000 feet
quiz.why: High-performance means an engine of more than 200 horsepower [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)(1)]].

quiz.q: No person may act as a crewmember within how many hours after drinking alcohol?
quiz.why: Within 8 hours after consumption of any alcoholic beverage [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: Under the current BasicMed rule, which flight is allowed?
options: 6 passengers in a 7-seat airplane with max takeoff weight 5,800 lb at 9,500 ft
A flight at FL190
A flight at 260 knots indicated
7 passengers in an 8-seat airplane
quiz.why: BasicMed allows aircraft authorized for not more than 7 occupants and 12,500 lb, with no more than 6 passengers, at or below 18,000 ft MSL and 250 KIAS [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].

quiz.q: Under BasicMed, the medical education course must be completed within the previous:
options: 12 calendar months
24 calendar months
48 calendar months
60 calendar months
quiz.why: The course must be done within 24 calendar months; the physician exam within 48 calendar months [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)-(D)]].

quiz.q: Which must a private pilot have in physical possession or readily accessible when acting as PIC (using an FAA medical)?
options: Pilot certificate and logbook
Pilot certificate, medical certificate, and photo ID
Medical certificate only
Logbook and photo ID
quiz.why: 61.3 requires the pilot certificate, an acceptable photo ID, and the medical certificate [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]], [[60:189|61.3(c)]].

quiz.q: Which best describes the difference between currency and proficiency?
options: They mean the same thing
Currency is meeting the legal minimums; proficiency is the ability to handle the flight's conditions
Proficiency is a legal requirement; currency is optional
Currency only applies to instrument pilots
quiz.why: Currency is logging the required events; proficiency is the ability to manage the conditions expected on the flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

quiz.q: According to AC 90-109A, what is the best way to get transition training for an unfamiliar airplane?
options: In the specific airplane you will fly, with an instructor who has recent experience in that make and model
In any airplane of the same category and class
In a simulator only
Self-study of the POH; no flight training is needed if you are current
quiz.why: The AC's first choice is the specific airplane you plan to fly, with a well-qualified instructor who preferably has recent make-and-model experience; second is the same make and model [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]].

takeaways: Your certificate never expires; your flight review (24 calendar months), landings (90 days), and medical do.
Passengers need 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days; at night they must be full stops 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
Private pilots may not fly for hire; pay at least your pro rata share of costs.
Complex, high-performance (more than 200 HP), and tailwheel each need an endorsement.
Carry your pilot certificate, photo ID, and medical (or driver's license for BasicMed), and ground yourself if not fit.
Legal is the minimum. Ask if you are proficient for this flight, in this airplane, with these avionics.
cfi_notes: Students confuse 'calendar months' with exact dates. Drill several flight review and medical expiration dates.
Common error: thinking touch-and-goes count for night currency. They must be full stops (61.57(b)).
Common error: thinking a first-class medical 'expires' for everything after 6 or 12 months. It steps down to private privileges for the 24/60-month period (61.23(d)).
Examiners often probe complex vs high-performance with a fixed-gear, 230 HP airplane, and cost-sharing math.

BasicMed numbers changed: AC 68-1A (2017) still shows 6 occupants / 6,000 lb / 5 passengers. The 14 CFR text in our files (as of 10/08/2026) says 7 / 12,500 / 6. Teach the regulation and confirm the current eCFR before each checkride season.
Use the scenario to show a pilot can be legal yet not proficient. Have the student state personal minimums out loud.
PHAK 17-2 states first-class duration as 'one year if 40 or younger'; the regulation table says under age 40. Teach from 14 CFR 61.23(d).
gaps: BasicMed: AC 68-1A (res 36, dated 5/3/17) gives older limits (6 occupants, 6,000 lb, 5 passengers, no compensation) that differ from the current 14 CFR 61.113(i) in res 35 (7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers). Lesson uses the regulation; AC 68-1A may be outdated.
Endorsement wording (AC 61-65K) for flight review, high-performance, complex, and tailwheel was not included; see res 12 if CFIs need sample text.
Aircraft-specific transition details (POH/AFM, specific avionics) depend on the training airplane and are not covered by these sources.

activities.title: Can I be PIC? Put the checklist in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the 8 checks in the order from the checkride skill, then tap Check.
steps: Certificate: right certificate, category, and class?
Passengers: 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days? Night full stops?
Medical: valid at your age, or BasicMed met?
Fitness: any condition, medication, or alcohol issue?
Documents: certificate, photo ID, medical or driver's license?
Purpose: any compensation? Cost sharing pro rata?

cards.s: A private pilot certificate expires after 24 months.
cards.why: No. The certificate has no expiration date. What expires is your currency and your medical [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19]].

cards.s: A checkride for a new rating counts as a flight review.
You may fly as a crewmember 6 hours after your last drink if you feel fine.
cards.why: No. The wait is 8 hours, and you must also be under 0.04 alcohol concentration and not under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].

cards.s: Landings in a Cessna 152 can count toward carrying passengers in a Cessna 172.
cards.why: Yes. The rule counts by category and class, not make and model, though the FAA recommends getting current in each one [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]].

cards.s: Day passenger currency requires all 3 landings to be to a full stop.
cards.why: No. Full stops are required at night, and in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a) and (b)]].

final_quiz.q: Your last flight review was signed on August 22, 2024. Today is August 29, 2026. Can you act as PIC today?
options: Yes. It is good through August 31, 2026.
No. It ran out on August 22, 2026.
No. It ran out on July 31, 2026.
Yes. It is good until August 22, 2027.
final_quiz.why: The flight review counts in calendar months. A review done in August 2024 lasts through the last day of August 2026 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. On September 1, 2026 you need a new one.

final_quiz.q: You want to carry friends 2 hours after sunset tonight. Which recent landings, all in the same category and class, make you legal?
options: 3 touch-and-go landings 2 hours after sunset, 20 days ago
3 full-stop landings 90 minutes after sunset, 60 days ago
3 full-stop landings 30 minutes after sunset, 10 days ago
3 full-stop landings 2 hours after sunset, 95 days ago
final_quiz.why: Night landings must be to a full stop, between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise, within the preceding 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]]. Touch-and-goes, landings only 30 minutes after sunset, and landings 95 days ago do not count.

final_quiz.q: You fly 2 friends to a lake. Fuel, oil, and rental total $360. Your friends offer to pay all of it. What is the least you must pay?
final_quiz.why: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share. With 3 people on board, that is $360 divided by 3, or $120 [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]].

final_quiz.q: You are a private pilot with 150 hours. Which flight may you act as PIC for?
options: Flying a company client to a meeting for a $200 fee
Showing an airplane to a buyer as an aircraft salesman
Flying yourself to a work meeting, when the flight is only incidental to your job and no one is carried for hire
A paid aerial photo flight for a local realtor
final_quiz.why: A private pilot may not fly for compensation or hire, except for flights only incidental to a business or job that carry no passengers or property for hire [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]], [[60:308|61.113(b)]]. Demonstrating airplanes as a salesman needs at least 200 hours [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(f)]].

final_quiz.q: A club airplane has a 180 HP engine, retractable landing gear, flaps, and a constant-speed propeller. Which endorsement do you need to act as PIC?
options: Complex only
High-performance only
Both complex and high-performance
None, since you hold an ASEL rating
final_quiz.why: Retractable gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller make it complex [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]], so you need the complex endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]]. It is not high-performance, because 180 HP is not more than 200 HP [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].

final_quiz.q: You have a tailwheel endorsement. In the last 60 days you made 5 touch-and-go landings in a tailwheel airplane and 3 full-stop landings in a tricycle-gear Cessna. Can you take a passenger in the tailwheel airplane today?
options: Yes. You have more than 3 landings in 90 days.
Yes. The Cessna landings count because it is the same class.
Yes, but only if the passenger is also a pilot.
No. You need 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings in a tailwheel airplane.
final_quiz.why: To carry persons in a tailwheel airplane, the 3 takeoffs and landings must be to a full stop in an airplane with a tailwheel [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]]. Touch-and-goes and tricycle-gear landings do not count for it.

final_quiz.q: Your takeoff is planned for 0600. Under the 8-hour rule, what is the latest time you may finish your last drink?
options: 2200 the night before
Midnight
1800 the night before
final_quiz.why: No one may act as a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol, and 0600 minus 8 hours is 2200 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]]. You must also be below 0.04 and not under the influence, and the PHAK says it is wise to be more conservative than the rules [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

final_quiz.q: Last night you took an allergy pill with diphenhydramine. This morning you still feel drowsy. Your medical is current. What should you do?
options: Fly, because your medical certificate is valid
Fly solo only, with no passengers
Do not fly until the drowsiness is gone, because the drug affects your faculties
Fly, as long as 8 hours have passed since the pill
final_quiz.why: No one may act as a crewmember while using a drug that affects their faculties in any way contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]]. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness that can last a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. A valid medical does not make you fit to fly.

final_quiz.q: You are 45. Your first-class medical exam was in April 2026. You fly only as a private pilot. Through what date can you use it?
options: April 30, 2028
October 31, 2026
April 30, 2027
April 30, 2031
final_quiz.why: For private privileges, a first-class medical from an exam at age 40 or older lasts to the end of the 24th month after the exam month [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(v)]]. October 31, 2026 is only the limit for ATP pilot in command privileges.

final_quiz.q: Which of these pilots may NOT fly under BasicMed?
options: A pilot whose last FAA medical expired in 2015
A pilot who took the BasicMed course 20 calendar months ago
A pilot whose physician exam was 40 calendar months ago
A pilot whose most recent FAA medical application was completed and denied
final_quiz.why: Your most recent medical application cannot have been completed and denied [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(iv)]]. An expired medical is fine if it was held after July 14, 2006, the course must be within 24 calendar months, and the exam within 48 [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)-(ii)]].

final_quiz.q: You fly under BasicMed. You left your driver's license at home, but you have your passport and pilot certificate. Can you act as PIC?
options: Yes. A passport is an accepted photo ID.
No. BasicMed needs a U.S. driver's license, and a passport cannot replace it.
Yes, if your exam checklist is in your logbook.
Yes, but only with no passengers.
final_quiz.why: Under BasicMed, the U.S. driver's license takes the place of the medical certificate [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)]]. A passport works as photo ID, but not in place of the driver's license [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]]. The license must be in your possession when you fly [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

final_quiz.q: You are legally current but have not flown in 6 weeks. Your recent landings were in light winds on a long runway. Friends want to fly to a short strip with gusty winds. What is the best choice?
options: Go, because being current means you are ready
Go, and lower your personal minimums so the flight fits
Practice first, solo or with an instructor, and raise your personal minimums for this flight
Go, but tell your friends to expect a firm landing
final_quiz.why: The landing rules are minimums. A pilot used to light winds and long runways should get more practice before carrying passengers in stronger winds or on short runways [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]]. Not flying for several weeks is a reason to raise personal minimums, never lower them to finish a flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot with many hours in a fast, glass-cockpit airplane rents a slow, light, older airplane for the first time. What does AC 90-109A say?
options: Moving down in performance has as much risk as moving up, so get transition training
No training is needed when moving to a simpler airplane
Read the POH; flying skills carry over to slower airplanes
Training is needed only if the new airplane is complex
final_quiz.why: Accident data shows as much risk in moving down in performance as in moving up. Skills from fast airplanes do not prepare a pilot for a low-inertia, high-drag airplane [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise, the autopilot suddenly turns off your course and you are not sure why. What should you do?
options: Keep reprogramming the GPS until the autopilot follows it
Reduce the level of automation and fly the airplane by hand if needed
Wait a few minutes to see if it fixes itself
Turn on more autopilot modes to take back control
final_quiz.why: If the automation does not do what you expect, reduce the level of automation, fly manually, and take time to sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
